# Freelance Feedback and Revision Rounds Kit

Endless revisions rarely come from difficult clients. They come from feedback that arrives in pieces, from five people, in five places, saying "can it pop a bit more?" This kit fixes the feedback itself, so two rounds of revisions really are two rounds.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `revision-policy.md` | How many rounds to include, what counts as a revision versus a change, and plain-English wording for your proposal | Once, when you set up your proposal template |
| `feedback-form.md` | A one-page feedback form the client fills in for each round | Send with every draft |
| `how-to-give-feedback-guide.md` | A short guide you send clients at kickoff on how to give feedback that gets results | At the start of each project |
| `revision-emails.md` | 9 ready-to-send emails for every feedback problem you'll hit | Whenever feedback goes sideways |
| `vague-feedback-decoder.md` | 15 common vague comments and the exact question to ask back | Any time you get "make it pop" |
| `worked-example.md` | A full project run with this system, round by round | Read once before your next project |
| `revision-log.csv` | A log of every round: what was asked, what counted, what was billed | Keep one per project |

## How to set it up in 30 minutes

1. **Decide your rounds (10 min).** Read `revision-policy.md` and pick how many rounds each of your services includes. Paste the short policy into your proposal template.
2. **Make the form yours (10 min).** Copy `feedback-form.md` into a document or shared file with your name on it. Delete any questions that don't fit your work.
3. **Save the emails (10 min).** Put the emails from `revision-emails.md` into your email app as templates.

## The four rules that make this work

1. **One round = one set of consolidated feedback from one person.** Not one email; one complete set. If comments arrive in pieces, the round isn't done until the client says it is.
2. **Feedback goes in one place.** The form, a single document, or a single email. Not chat, plus email, plus a call, plus a comment on the file.
3. **Revisions refine; changes redirect.** "Make the headline shorter" is a revision. "Actually, can we target a different audience?" is a change, and it's quoted separately.
4. **Every round is logged.** A one-line note per round makes the "we've used both rounds" conversation calm and factual instead of awkward.

## Who it's for

Designers, writers, developers, video editors, illustrators, marketers: anyone who sends drafts to a client and waits for feedback. The examples use design and copywriting, but every template works with small wording changes.

## A note on the policy wording

The wording in `revision-policy.md` is a plain-English starting point, not legal advice. For formal contracts or large projects, have it checked by someone qualified where you work.

# Feedback Form: [Project name], Draft [number]

**From:** [approver's name]
**Date sent:** [date]
**This is round [1] of [2] included.**

Please fill this in once, with everyone's comments combined. When you send it, I'll start on the next draft. Anything that arrives after this goes into the next round, so take the time you need and send it when it's complete.

---

## 1. Overall, how close is this?

Pick one:

- [ ] **Nearly there.** Small tweaks only.
- [ ] **Right direction.** Some sections need real work.
- [ ] **Not right yet.** The overall direction needs to change. (Please explain in section 2, and I'll suggest a short call.)

## 2. What's working?

List what you want to **keep**. This matters as much as what to change: it stops good parts getting lost in the next draft.

1.
2.
3.

## 3. What needs to change?

One line per change. Be as specific as you can about **where** (page, section, timestamp, paragraph) and **why** (what's not working for you or your customers). You don't need to suggest the fix; the "why" is what I need most.

| # | Where | What's not working | Why it matters | Must have or nice to have? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| 3 | | | | |
| 4 | | | | |
| 5 | | | | |
| 6 | | | | |
| 7 | | | | |
| 8 | | | | |

## 4. Did anyone disagree?

If two people asked for opposite things, list both here with **your decision** on which way to go. If you'd like my opinion first, say so and I'll give a recommendation before I start.

| Topic | Person A wants | Person B wants | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

## 5. Anything new since the brief?

Has anything changed since we started: audience, deadline, budget, a new product, a new person involved? New things are great to know about, but they may be outside the agreed scope, so I'll come back to you with options before acting on them.

-

## 6. Confirm

- [ ] Everyone who needs to see this draft has seen it.
- [ ] These comments are complete for this round.
- [ ] [Approver's name] has made the final call where people disagreed.

Thank you! Next draft will be with you by [date].

# How to Give Feedback That Gets You Great Work

*A one-page guide for clients. Send it at kickoff, with your name and project details added.*

Hi [client name],

You'll see your first draft of [project] on [date]. Here's how to get the most out of each round of feedback. It takes five minutes to read and usually saves a week of back-and-forth.

## 1. Pick one approver

Choose one person to collect everyone's comments and make the final calls. That's usually you. When feedback comes from several people separately, it often contradicts itself, and I end up guessing who to follow.

## 2. Collect everything, then send once

Each round includes everyone's feedback, sent together. Please don't send comments as they occur to you. Wait until everyone has looked, combine it, and send it in one go using the feedback form. If something comes up after you've sent it, I'll add it to the next round.

## 3. Tell me the problem, not the fix

"Change the button to green" might solve the problem, or it might not. "People won't notice the button" tells me what's actually wrong, and I can suggest the best fix, which may be size or position rather than color. You're the expert on your business and customers. I'm the expert on [design / writing / your craft]. Feedback works best when each of us does our part.

## 4. Say what's working

It's easy to list only problems. But if you don't tell me what you love, I might change it while fixing something else.

## 5. Be specific about where

"The second paragraph on the About page" is much faster to act on than "some of the wording".

## 6. Think about your customer, not just your taste

Before each comment, it helps to ask: "Would my customer care about this?" Some personal preferences matter (it's your business), but the ones that serve your customers matter most.

## 7. Big changes are fine, just tell me early

If something has changed since the brief (new audience, new direction, new deadline), tell me as soon as you know. It may be outside what we agreed, so I'll give you options and a quote before doing anything, but it's always cheaper to change direction early.

## 8. Please reply within [5] working days

Your timeline depends on it. If you need longer, just let me know and we'll adjust the dates.

---

**This project includes [2] rounds of revisions.** Extra rounds are available at [$amount] each. I'll always tell you before you use one.

Thanks, I'm looking forward to it.

[Your name]
files.revision-emails.md:
# Revision Emails: 9 Ready-to-Send Templates

Replace everything in [square brackets]. Tone: calm, friendly, factual. You're describing how the project works, not scolding anyone.

---

## 1. Sending a draft

**Subject:** [Project]: draft [1] ready for your feedback

Hi [name],

Draft [1] of [project] is here: [where to find it].

A quick note on what I focused on: [1-2 sentences on the thinking behind the draft, so they review it against the goal, not their mood].

When you're ready, please gather everyone's comments and send them in one go using the feedback form [attached / linked]. This is round [1] of [2] included. If you can get it to me by [date, 5 working days out], I'll have the next draft to you by [date].

[Your name]

---

## 2. Feedback is arriving in pieces

**Subject:** Re: [project] feedback

Hi [name],

Thanks for these comments. I can see a few have come through [over email and chat / from different people] today. So I don't start on half the picture and redo it later, I'll wait until you've got everything together.

Could you let me know when this round is complete, ideally in the feedback form so it's all in one place? I'll start the next draft as soon as I hear from you.

[Your name]

---

## 3. Two people want opposite things

**Subject:** Re: [project] feedback: one decision needed

Hi [name],

Thanks for the feedback. Before I start, there's one place where I've had two different directions:

- [Person A] would like [X].
- [Person B] would like [Y].

My recommendation is [X/Y], because [one-sentence reason tied to the project goal]. But it's your call. Which would you like me to go with?

Everything else is clear and I'm ready to go once I hear back.

[Your name]

---

## 4. Feedback is vague

**Subject:** Re: [project] feedback

Hi [name],

Thanks, this is helpful. On a couple of points I want to be sure I get it right rather than guess:

- When you say "[vague comment]", is it more that [option A] or [option B]?
- For "[vague comment]", could you point me to an example of something that feels right to you? It doesn't have to be in your industry.

(See `vague-feedback-decoder.md` for the right question to ask for each common comment.)

[Your name]

---

## 5. A request that's a change, not a revision

**Subject:** Re: [project]: about the new [section/idea]

Hi [name],

[New idea] sounds like a good addition. It's outside the brief we agreed, so rather than fold it into this round I'll treat it separately so it doesn't slow down the rest:

- **Option 1:** Add it now for [$amount], which moves delivery to [date].
- **Option 2:** Finish the current project as planned and do [new idea] as a follow-on for [$amount].
- **Option 3:** Leave it out for now.

The rest of your feedback is all within this round and I'm working on it now.

[Your name]

---

## 6. The last included round is next

**Subject:** [Project]: draft [2] ready (final included round)

Hi [name],

Draft [2] is here: [link].

Just so you know, this is the last of the [2] included rounds, so it's worth taking a little extra time to gather everything before you send it. If you need more rounds after this, they're [$amount] each, and I'll always check with you before starting one.

Looking forward to hearing what you think.

[Your name]

---

## 7. Included rounds are used up and more changes arrive

**Subject:** Re: [project] more changes

Hi [name],

Thanks for these. We've now used both included rounds (round 1 on [date], round 2 on [date]), so this would be an extra round at [$amount].

If you'd like to go ahead, just reply "yes" and I'll start; the new draft would be with you by [date]. If any of these are small enough to make yourself, I'm happy to send you the editable file instead.

[Your name]

---

## 8. Feedback has gone quiet

Send after the feedback window has passed.

**Subject:** [Project]: checking in on draft [number]

Hi [name],

Just checking in on draft [number], which I sent on [date]. No pressure at all; I know things get busy. To keep the project on track:

- If you've got feedback, send it whenever it's ready and the next draft will follow [X] working days later.
- If you're happy as it is, just reply "approved" and I'll [send final files / move to the next stage].

If I haven't heard by [date, per the policy], I'll treat the draft as approved and send the final files and invoice, as in our agreement.

[Your name]

---

## 9. Asking for final approval

**Subject:** [Project]: ready for final approval

Hi [name],

Here's the final version of [project]: [link]. It includes everything from the last round.

If you're happy, could you reply with "approved"? I'll then send [final files / handover notes] and the final invoice. After approval, any further changes are new work, so let me know now if anything is still on your mind.

It's been a pleasure working on this.

[Your name]

files.revision-policy.md:
# Your Revision Policy

## Step 1: Decide how many rounds to include

Too few rounds and clients feel nervous about signing. Too many and they stop thinking hard about each one. A common starting point:

| Type of work | Rounds included | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Small, well-defined job (a social graphic, a 500-word post) | 1 | Little room for interpretation |
| Standard project (a logo, website copy, a short video) | 2 | One to steer, one to polish |
| Large or exploratory project (brand identity, full website) | 2 per stage | Rounds reset at each stage (concepts, then design, then build) |
| Retainer work | 1-2 per piece | Set in the retainer terms |

Most people find **two rounds per stage** covers almost every project when the feedback is good. The rest of this kit is about making the feedback good.

## Step 2: Define a round

Put this definition in writing. It's the most useful sentence in the whole policy.

> **A round** is one complete, consolidated set of feedback on a draft, sent in one place by the project's approver. When I receive it, I make the changes and send the next draft. Comments that arrive after a round has been sent are included in the next round.

## Step 3: Separate revisions from changes

| A revision (included) | A change (quoted separately) |
|---|---|
| Adjusts what's there | Replaces what's there |
| "Shorten the intro" | "Let's add a pricing page" |
| "Try the blue a shade darker" | "Can we see a completely new direction?" |
| "Swap these two sections" | "We've changed our target customer" |
| "This sentence sounds stiff" | "Our CEO wants to rewrite the whole thing in her voice" |
| Fixing something I got wrong | Something new the client has decided since the brief |

A good test: **could the change have been predicted from the original brief?** If yes, it's a revision. If it comes from new information, a new idea or a new decision, it's a change.

Mistakes you made don't count as a round, ever. Fix them for free and say so; it builds trust.

## Step 4: Set the price of extra rounds

Decide this before the project, not in the middle of it. Two common options:

- **Hourly:** extra rounds are billed at [your hourly rate], with an estimate sent before you start.
- **Per round:** each extra round is a fixed [$amount], usually 10-15% of the project price.

Per round is simpler for the client to say yes to.

## Step 5: Set a feedback window

Long silences kill projects and let feedback pile up. Add a window, for example **5 working days** per round. If feedback doesn't arrive in that time, the timeline moves, and after [15] working days with no reply, the draft is treated as approved.

## Policy wording

### Short version (for proposals)

> **Revisions.** This project includes [2] rounds of revisions [per stage]. A round is one complete, consolidated set of feedback from [approver's name], sent in one place, usually the feedback form I'll share with each draft. Revisions adjust the agreed work; new requests or changes of direction are quoted separately before I start them. Additional rounds are [$amount] each. Please send feedback within [5] working days of each draft so we stay on schedule.

### Full version (for contracts and terms)

**1. Included rounds.** The project includes the number of revision rounds stated in the proposal. Rounds not used in one stage do not carry over to the next stage.

**2. What a round is.** A round is one complete, consolidated set of feedback on a draft, sent in one place by the approver named in the proposal. Feedback received after a round has been submitted is included in the following round.

**3. The approver.** The client names one approver who collects feedback from everyone else and makes final decisions. Feedback from anyone else is passed through the approver.

**4. Revisions and changes.** A revision adjusts work within the agreed brief. A change adds to, removes from, or redirects the agreed brief. Changes are quoted in writing before work on them starts, and may affect the timeline.

**5. Corrections.** Corrections of errors on my part are not counted as a revision round.

**6. Extra rounds.** Rounds beyond those included are charged at [$amount per round / my hourly rate of $X], with an estimate given before work starts.

**7. Feedback window.** Feedback is due within [5] working days of each draft. Late feedback moves the delivery date by at least the same amount. If no feedback is received within [15] working days, the draft is treated as approved and the next stage or final invoice follows.

**8. Final approval.** Approval of the final draft, in writing (an email is fine), completes the project. Changes after approval are new work.

# Vague Feedback Decoder

Vague feedback isn't bad feedback. It's a real reaction that the client doesn't have words for yet. Your job is to turn it into something you can act on with one good question. Never guess: a guess usually burns a whole round.

| They say | What it often means | Ask back |
|---|---|---|
| "Make it pop." | It feels flat or doesn't grab attention. Could be contrast, size, color, or a weak headline. | "Is it the first thing you see that's not grabbing you, or the page as a whole feeling a bit quiet?" |
| "It doesn't feel right." | Something conflicts with how they see their brand, but they can't name it. | "If this were a person, how would you describe them? And how would you describe your brand as a person?" |
| "Can it be more modern?" | It reminds them of something dated, or a competitor looks fresher. | "Could you send me one or two examples that feel modern to you? Anything, even outside your industry." |
| "It's too busy." | Too many elements competing; nothing leads. | "If someone only saw one thing here, what should it be?" |
| "It's too plain." | Not enough personality or visual interest. | "Is it missing warmth, energy, or polish? Which of those is closest?" |
| "Make it more professional." | Tone or style feels casual for their audience. | "Who's the most important person who'll see this, and what would make them trust you more?" |
| "It needs more energy." | Pace, language or visuals feel slow. | "Is that in the words, the visuals, or both?" |
| "I'll know it when I see it." | They don't have a clear picture yet. | "Let's narrow it down: of these three quick directions, which is closest?" (Send rough options, not full drafts.) |
| "Can you try a few options?" | They're unsure and hope options will decide for them. | "Happy to. What's the one thing the options should differ on, so you can compare them?" |
| "My partner/boss doesn't like it." | Someone with influence hasn't seen the brief. | "What specifically didn't work for them? And would it help if I talked them through the thinking?" |
| "It's not what I imagined." | The brief and their mental picture differ. | "What did you imagine? Even rough words or a sketch help." |
| "Can it be warmer?" | Feels cold, corporate, or distant. | "Warmer in the colors, the words, or the photos? Or all three?" |
| "It's a bit long." | They lost interest somewhere. | "Where did your attention start to drift?" |
| "Can we tweak the wording?" | Something specific is bothering them. | "Which sentence stood out to you first?" |
| "Just a few small changes." | Could be small, could be big. | "Great, send them over in the form and I'll let you know if any fall outside this round." |

## Three habits that prevent vague feedback

1. **Explain the thinking with every draft.** One or two sentences: "I went with a calm, spacious layout because your customers are stressed when they arrive." Clients give better feedback when they know what the draft is trying to do.
2. **Ask for what's working first.** The form does this. It anchors the client in specifics.
3. **Show references early.** At the start, ask for three examples they like and three they don't. It saves a round almost every time.

# Worked Example: One Project, Two Rounds, No Drama

The names and numbers are made up; the method is the one in this kit.

## The setup

Jonas is a freelance designer. A small bakery chain hires him to design a one-page menu and a matching A5 flyer for **$1,400**. His proposal includes:

- **2 rounds of revisions**, defined as "one consolidated set of feedback from the approver".
- **Extra rounds at $180** each (about 13% of the project).
- A **5-working-day** feedback window.
- **Approver:** Priya, the operations manager.

At kickoff, Jonas sends Priya the client guide (`how-to-give-feedback-guide.md`) and asks for three examples she likes and three she doesn't.

## Round 1

Jonas sends draft 1 with email 1, explaining: "I've used a lot of white space and big, simple prices, because people read menus from the queue, at a distance."

**What came back.** Within an hour, the owner, Marco, emails directly: "Love it but can the logo be bigger?" Later that day, a store manager adds a chat message: "Can we add the gluten-free symbols?"

Jonas doesn't start. He sends email 2 to Priya: "I'll wait until you've got everyone's feedback together; just let me know when this round is complete."

Two days later, Priya sends the completed form:

| # | Where | What's not working | Why | Must/nice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Header | Logo feels small | Marco wants brand recognition from the street | Must |
| 2 | Pastries section | No allergen info | Customers ask staff every day | Must |
| 3 | Prices | Font feels "too modern" | Doesn't match the shop's handmade feel | Must |
| 4 | Flyer | Could it include a loyalty card offer? | New idea from marketing | Nice |

In section 4 (disagreements), she writes: "Store manager wanted brown, Marco wants the green kept. Decision: keep green."

**How Jonas sorts it:**

- Items 1-3 are **revisions**: they adjust the agreed design. Included.
- Item 3 is vague ("too modern"). He uses the decoder and asks: "Could you send one or two examples of lettering that feels right for the shop?" Priya sends a photo of their hand-painted window sign. Now it's clear.
- Item 4 is a **change**: a loyalty offer wasn't in the brief and needs new copy and a new layout block. He sends email 5 with three options. Priya picks "do it as a follow-on" for **$250**.

Jonas logs round 1 in `revision-log.csv`.

## Round 2

Jonas sends draft 2 with email 6 ("this is the last included round"). Priya takes four days, gathers everyone, and sends back two small items: tighten the spacing between sections, and fix a typo in "croissant" that Jonas made.

- The spacing is a revision: round 2.
- The typo was Jonas's mistake: fixed free, not counted. He says so: "Typo fixed. That one was mine, so it doesn't count toward anything."

## After round 2

A week later, Marco emails: "Could we try the whole thing in brown after all?"

Jonas sends email 7: "We've used both included rounds (round 1 on the 4th, round 2 on the 11th), so this would be an extra round at $180." Marco says yes. Because the rounds were logged and the price was agreed up front, it's a two-line exchange, not a negotiation.

Then Jonas sends email 9 for final approval. Priya replies "approved."

## The numbers

| | Amount |
|---|---|
| Original project | $1,400 |
| Extra round (brown version) | $180 |
| Follow-on: loyalty card block | $250 |
| **Total billed** | **$1,830** |
| Rounds of feedback | 3 (2 included, 1 paid) |
| Unpaid rework from piecemeal feedback | none |

Without the system, Jonas's previous menu project for another client went through **six** informal rounds over five weeks, all within the original fee.

## What the log looked like

| round | date_sent | date_feedback | from | items | revisions | changes_quoted | my_errors_fixed | included_or_paid | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-05-01 | 2026-05-04 | Priya | 4 | 3 | 1 (loyalty block, $250 follow-on) | 0 | included | waited for consolidated feedback |
| 2 | 2026-05-07 | 2026-05-11 | Priya | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | included | typo fixed free |
| 3 | 2026-05-18 | 2026-05-19 | Marco via Priya | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | paid $180 | brown version |
